findings.title: Blocklist match counter is inflated because the check writes from inside validation
findings.body: `should_block?` increments `match_count` and saves the row, but it is called from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, which runs on every `valid?` or `save` of a User whose email changed. In `UsersController#create` the code calls `user.valid?` (line ~168) and then `user.save` (line ~172), so one blocked signup attempt increments `match_count` twice, and any other validation call adds more. The statistic therefore does not reflect the number of blocked attempts. Also, a validator that mutates blocklist state couples every model using `validates :email, email: true` to that side effect. Record the match once in the controller or a single save path, and keep validation read-only.

findings.title: Blocklist lookup is case-sensitive, so case variants bypass a blocked address
findings.body: `should_block?` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, an exact, case-sensitive match. Nothing normalizes the address first: `User.new_from_params` assigns `params[:email]` verbatim, and the domain restriction in the same validator is case-insensitive (`Regexp.new(..., true)`). If 'spam@example.com' is blocked, a signup with 'Spam@Example.com' passes validation and is stored. The unique index on blocked_emails is also case-sensitive, so case variants can coexist as separate entries. Normalize both the stored value and the lookup key (for example with Email.downcase, which the codebase already uses for lookups).

findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write loses match_count increments under concurrency
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` reads the count into Ruby, increments it, and writes it back. Two concurrent signup attempts that read the same value both write value+1, so an increment is lost. `save` also reruns validations, including the uniqueness query, just to bump a counter. Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` or `update_counters`.

findings.title: rejectedEmails is never cleared, so any server email error blocks that address until reload
findings.body: Every response with `errors.email` pushes the address into `rejectedEmails`, and `emailValidation` then fails that exact address (line 69) for the controller's lifetime. That includes errors that are not about the blocklist, such as 'has already been taken'. The field then shows the generic `user.email.invalid` reason for an address that is well-formed but registered, and submit stays disabled for it even if the server-side condition changes (for example, an admin removes the blocklist entry). Consider clearing the list when the email changes or limiting it to the blocked-email error.

findings.title: New errors and values keys in the failed-signup response have no spec
findings.body: The failed-create JSON now includes `errors` and `values`, and the new client code depends on that shape (`result.errors.email && result.values`). No request or controller spec in this PR checks these keys, so renaming or dropping them would silently break the rejected-email handling in the frontend.

findings.title: Moved domain whitelist/blacklist logic and the real blocklist path are untested here
findings.body: The whitelist and blacklist checks were moved from User into EmailValidator in this PR, but this spec only covers the blocked-email branch, and it stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so the real lookup is never exercised. Nothing in this PR checks the domain restrictions through the new validator, the short-circuit (no blocklist lookup once a domain error is added), or case-insensitive matching. Regressions in the moved logic or the case-sensitivity issue would not be caught by these specs.
